identity.plain_name: A short pipe with sharp ridges round it that you push a soft tube over; the ridges bite into the inside of the tube so it seals and won't pull off, and a clip round the tube holds it on harder
identity.term: Hose barb (barbed fitting, barbed tube connector)
aliases: barbed fitting, barb fitting, barbed connector, barb connector, hose barb connector (ISM; Tameson)
hose tail or hosetail (UK; a Printables model title uses 'Hose Barb Hosetail')
hose nipple, hose spigot [uncertain] (hose nipple appears in Wikipedia's Hose clamp article)
'Christmas-tree' barb: the older style with several barbs of increasing size (Beswick)
single-barb or 'line contact' barb (Beswick; Hydraulics & Pneumatics)
hose splicer, hose coupler, hose mender, barb-to-barb reducer, barb tee, barb wye (names for fittings with a barb on each end; Printables model titles)
slip-in fitting, barbed insert fitting (drip irrigation; DripWorks)
identity.one_liner: A ridged spigot (hose barb) that a soft tube is stretched over, so the tube's own elasticity grips the ridges and seals the joint for low-pressure air, water or other fluids, with an optional clamp or cable tie behind the barb for extra hold.
identity.complexity: Single piece, plus the tube and an optional clamp. Parts: a hollow spigot with one or more ridges (barbs), each with a gentle slope and a sharp back edge; a plain cylindrical stem behind the barb for the tube to relax onto; and on the other end another barb, a thread, a flange or a tee (Tameson; ISM). Retention device if used: a worm-drive, spring, wire or ear clamp, or a cable tie (Wikipedia, Hose clamp; Qosina).
identity.how_it_works: The tube is pushed up the slope of the barb, stretching it wider than its own inside diameter; once past the sharp edge it springs back and squeezes the plain stem behind it (ISM). That squeeze makes the seal, and the sharp edge makes a line of high contact pressure that grips the tube (Beswick). Pulling on the tube makes it get thinner and grip even tighter, but a pressure spike swells the tube and can loosen it, which is why a clamp is added for higher pressure (ISM; Qosina). A clamp placed just behind the barb also blocks the tube from sliding off, because the clamp would have to stretch over the barb (Wikipedia, Hose clamp).

job: seal it, or pass cables or fluid through: joins a soft tube to a fitting or a device so air or liquid can pass without leaking
join and hold: holds the tube on against pulling and internal pressure
finder_attributes.motion: none: the tube is fixed to the barb (the soft tube itself can still bend)
finder_attributes.degrees_of_freedom: 0: once pushed on, the tube is held in place on the barb; it may be possible to twist the tube round the barb by hand, but it isn't meant to move
special_behaviour: one-way (moves freely one way, locks the other): only in the sense that the barb's slope lets the tube slide on easily while its sharp back edge resists pulling the tube off; pulling actually makes the tube grip tighter (ISM; Hydraulics & Pneumatics)
holding_principle: friction or clamping (force-fit): the stretched tube squeezes the barb stem, and a clamp adds more squeeze
shape (the parts interlock; form-fit): the tube relaxes behind the sharp barb edge, which hooks it; a clamp behind the barb also blocks the tube from sliding off (Wikipedia, Hose clamp)
finder_attributes.input_output: not applicable: it joins a tube and passes fluid, not motion
finder_attributes.removability: semi-permanent (can be undone but may damage parts): a well-matched barb is designed to be very hard to pull off (Beswick), so the tube end is often cut off; the fitting itself can usually be reused with a new tube (Tameson). Soft silicone tubing can often be worked off by hand [uncertain]
finder_attributes.reuse_cycles: a few times: the barb can be reused many times, but each removal usually costs a cut or stretched tube end (Tameson)
finder_attributes.tools_needed: None to push on (hot water or a hair dryer helps soften stiff tubing; Drip Depot). A knife or tube cutter for a square cut; pliers for spring clamps, a screwdriver or nut driver for worm-drive clamps, a special pincer tool for ear clamps (Wikipedia, Hose clamp); cable ties need only a cutter.
finder_attributes.seal: airtight or pressure: the stretched tube squeezing the plain stem behind the barb makes the seal, good for low pressures (ISM: 125 psi or lower); a clamp adds sealing force and resists blow-off (Beswick). Printed barbs are only as tight as their walls (Prusa Knowledge Base)
finder_attributes.load: light: holds a tube against pulling and low pressure. Strong against pull (the tube grips tighter; ISM), weaker against pressure spikes that swell the tube (ISM; Qosina). Metal and moulded barbs are strong in bending; printed barbs are weakest where the barb joins a flange or body and can snap there if the tube is levered sideways (Printables 1765791).
finder_attributes.adjustable: no: the grip is set by the barb size, the tube's hardness and the clamp; you can only tighten a screw clamp
finder_attributes.access_needed: end of a tube or shaft: you push the tube over the end of the barb, so you need the free end of the tube and room to push it on
finder_attributes.materials: Fittings: brass, stainless steel, nylon and other plastics such as polypropylene and PVDF (Kynar) (Tameson; ISM; Beswick). Tubing that suits barbs: soft, elastic tubing such as silicone, TPE, PVC and softer polyurethane (Qosina; Beswick); Clippard recommends 85A polyurethane for barbs but 95A for push-in fittings. Stiff tubing (nylon, polyethylene, PTFE, PEEK) suits push-to-connect or compression fittings better (Beswick), although drip-irrigation fittings are barbed inserts for polyethylene tubing (DripWorks). Printed barbs: PETG is a common choice for water; PLA only for dry indoor use (Printables 1829891); PP, ASA and PA11 nylon are also used (Printables 1829891, 1810917).
finder_attributes.maker_difficulty: easy: buy one for pennies, or print one in a single piece (the barb profile is support-free if the ridges are 45° cones; Printables 1765791); getting a printed one watertight needs extra walls and good settings

processes: off-the-shelf part: brass, stainless and plastic barbs, tees, wyes, reducers and barb-to-thread adapters
3D print (FDM): single-piece barbs and adapters, often printed standing up
3D print (resin) [uncertain]: possible for small fittings, but no test found
CNC: turned metal barbs on a lathe [uncertain]
making.print_in_place: yes: a barbed fitting is a single printed part with nothing to assemble; you just push the tube on (some multi-part designs, such as Printables 1436108, are printed in pieces and glued)
making.making_tips_3d_printing: 1) Orientation: most makers print barbs standing up, with the tube axis vertical, so each barb is a round ring of layers (Printables 1810917 printed this way in PLA and PA11 without supports; Printables 378315 printed a barb tee standing up with supports). Give the barbs a 45° slope on both sides so they print without supports (Printables 1765791 uses a '2x45° ridge profile'). 2) Leak-tight walls: use at least 3-4 perimeters, raise the nozzle temperature 5-10 °C and the extrusion multiplier 5-10%, keep layer height at no more than 60-65% of the nozzle size (Prusa Knowledge Base, Watertight prints); one drip-irrigation tee needed 6 perimeters to be water-tight under pressure (Printables 378315). Some designers print at 100% infill (Printables 1436108) or with walls thick enough to be solid. 3) Seam: set the seam to random, or scrape the seam smooth with a knife, because an aligned seam is a leak path along the barb (Printables 455268; Printables 1436108). 4) Material: PETG for water and outdoors; PLA only for dry indoor use (Printables 1829891); PLA starts to give at about 60 °C and PETG at about 80 °C (CNC Kitchen), so avoid printed barbs on hot water or engine coolant. 5) Strength: add a fillet or internal reinforcement where the barb joins a flange or body, the usual snapping point (Printables 1765791). 6) Sizing: measure the tube's inside diameter and make the barb a little larger; commercial barbs range from about 10% to 100% larger than the nominal tube ID depending on style (Qosina); parametric generators let you set the barb lip, count and length (Printables 1829891, 1767584; Printables 69154). 7) Hold: leave room behind the barb for a clamp or cable tie (Printables 1436108). 8) Don't use printed barbs for high pressure or fuel (Printables 1436108).
making.off_the_shelf_parts: Search for: 'hose barb', 'barbed fitting', 'barb x NPT' or 'barb x BSP' adapters ('hose tail' in the UK), 'barb tee', 'barb wye', 'barbed reducer', 'hose mender' or 'hose splicer', 'single-barb fitting', 'Luer to barb' (medical and lab), 'aquarium airline connector' (3/16 in, about 5 mm tubing; FishLab), 'drip irrigation barbed fitting' (DripWorks). Retention: 'worm drive hose clamp' ('Jubilee Clip' (brand) in the UK), 'spring hose clamp', 'wire hose clamp', 'ear clamp' or 'stepless ear clamp' (Oetiker (brand)) (Wikipedia, Hose clamp; Qosina), 'cable tie'. Tubing: 'silicone tubing', 'PVC tubing', 'polyurethane tubing 85A'.
rules_of_thumb: Barbed fittings are for low pressure: 'low-pressure (125 psi or lower) fluid, gas and air' (ISM, Barb Connectors in Depth); usually below 150 or 125 psi because the soft tubing is the limit (Beswick white paper).

Add a clamp when pressure approaches 80 to 100+ psi (depending on tube ID, wall and durometer); clamps also help with pressure pulses and heat (Beswick white paper). For drip irrigation, DripWorks advises stainless hose clamps above 20 psi.
Size a barb by the tube's inside diameter; push-in fittings are sized by the tube's outside diameter (Clippard).

Make the barb bigger than the tube's ID: Qosina's barb styles are 10-25%, 18-34%, 12-57%, 40-60% and up to 50-100% 'oversized' compared with the nominal tube ID. There are no consensus standards for barb sizes, so test with your tubing (Qosina).

Match barb and tube hardness: barbs suit soft tubing (Clippard recommends 85A polyurethane for barbs and 95A for push-in fittings; push-in fittings are typically used with 95 Shore A or harder tubing, Beswick). A barb for soft silicone needs a higher peak than one for stiff nylon (Hydraulics & Pneumatics).

One sharp barb with no mould parting line and a plain stem behind it for the tube to relax onto usually beats several barbs; if you do use several, space them far enough apart that the tube can close down behind each one (Hydraulics & Pneumatics, 'Plastic fittings: How many barbs are best?', 2004; Beswick).
Place the clamp or cable tie closely behind the barb (Qosina), so the tube can't slide off without the clamp stretching over the barb (Wikipedia, Hose clamp).
Worm-drive (screw) clamps are normally used on hoses 1/2 in diameter and up; smaller hoses use other clamps (Wikipedia, Hose clamp).
To fit stiff tubing, dip its end in hot (not boiling) water for about a count of 10 first (Drip Depot).
Printed watertight parts: at least 3-4 perimeters, +5-10 °C nozzle temperature, +5-10% extrusion multiplier (Prusa Knowledge Base, Watertight prints).

everyday_examples: Aquarium air-pump tubing and its little check valves and tees (standard 3/16 in, about 5 mm, airline tubing; FishLab)
Garden drip-irrigation fittings pushed into polyethylene tubing (DripWorks; Printables 378315)
PC water-cooling loops, with hoses clamped onto barb fittings (Wikipedia, Hose clamp; Wikimedia Commons photo)
Car heater and coolant hoses held on with spring or screw clamps (Wikipedia, Hose clamp)
The side arm of a lab vacuum flask or water aspirator (Wikipedia, Hose barb)
guidance.when_to_use: Use a hose barb to join soft, stretchy tubing (silicone, PVC, TPE, soft polyurethane) for low-pressure air, water, vacuum or other fluids when you want a cheap, compact joint that you set up once and leave: aquariums, garden watering, coolant loops, pumps, lab rigs, pneumatic toys and soft robots. It is small because it seals on the inside of the tube, it usually seals better than a push-in fitting on soft tube, and it costs less (Clippard; Beswick). It is also the easiest tube fitting to 3D print as one piece, e.g. to adapt one hose size or thread to another.
guidance.when_not_to_use: Don't use it for high pressure (well above about 100 psi), for pressure spikes, or where a blow-off would be dangerous: use compression or crimped fittings (Beswick; Wikipedia, Hose clamp). Don't use it with hard tubing such as nylon, polyethylene, PTFE or metal: use push-to-connect or compression fittings (Beswick; Clippard). If you need to connect and disconnect often, use a push-to-connect fitting or a quick-disconnect coupling (Clippard; Beswick). Don't use printed barbs for fuel, hot coolant or high pressure (Printables 1436108; CNC Kitchen).
guidance.environment_limits: The tubing sets most limits: pressure spikes swell it and loosen the grip (ISM), and heat softens it, which is why clamps are recommended for heat (Beswick). Check chemical compatibility and exposure to cleaners and sunlight for both tube and fitting (ISM). Printed barbs: PLA starts to give at about 60 °C, PETG at about 80 °C and ASA at about 110 °C (CNC Kitchen); PLA only for dry indoor use (Printables 1829891). Plastic tubing may harden and take a set on the barb over years, which makes it leak or crack when disturbed [uncertain].
guidance.safety_notes: A tube that blows off under pressure can spray hot or harmful fluid and whip about; clamp anything pressurised (Beswick) and don't use printed barbs for fuel or high pressure (Printables 1436108). In life-support or medical tubing a slipped-off tube can be dangerous (Hydraulics & Pneumatics). Take care when cutting stuck tubing off: Wikipedia warns that slitting a hose can scratch the barb and cause a leak, so cut away from yourself and from the barb [uncertain] (see common_failures).
guidance.common_failures: Tube splits or cracks: barb too sharp or too big for the tube, or the tube over-stretched (Tameson; ISM). Leaks: barb too small for the tube's ID (Tameson), a mould parting line or printed seam running along the barb (Hydraulics & Pneumatics; Printables 1436108), porous printed walls (Prusa Knowledge Base), or a scratched barb (Wikipedia, Hose clamp). Tube blows off: pressure spikes or too-high pressure with no clamp (ISM; Beswick). Tube pulls off: a shallow, rounded barb with stiff tubing (Qosina), or barbs spaced too closely for the tube to relax between them (Hydraulics & Pneumatics). Printed barb snaps at its base when the tube is levered sideways (Printables 1765791). Removal advice conflicts: Tameson says cut the tube so it spreads off the barb; Wikipedia's Hose clamp article says never slit stuck hoses because the knife can scratch the fitting.
related: Push-to-connect (push-in) fitting: a toothed collet grips the outside of stiffer tubing and an O-ring seals it; releases with a collar, so it is better for frequent reconnection (Clippard; Beswick)
Compression fitting: a nut squeezes a ferrule onto the outside of hard or metal tubing, for higher pressures (Beswick; Wikipedia, Hose clamp)
Quick-disconnect coupling: for many connect-disconnect cycles (Beswick)
Hose clamp: not a fitting on its own, but the add-on that seals and holds a hose on a barb (Wikipedia, Hose clamp)
O-ring seal: seals a rigid spigot inside a bore instead of stretching a tube
Cable gland: the equivalent idea for sealing a cable (not a tube) through a wall

media.diagram_idea: Cut-away of a tube being pushed onto a single barb: the tube stretches up the slope, springs down behind the sharp edge onto the plain stem (arrows showing the squeeze that seals), a hose clamp sitting just behind the barb, and a small inset showing a pressure spike swelling the tube (loosening) versus a pull thinning the tube (gripping harder).
